title: How increases are actually handled: large owners vs individual owners
important_limits: No official dataset records how San Francisco owners set rents in practice. No source located in this session documents institutional or individual owner behaviour with evidence. The 'practice' rows below are therefore left blank and marked unverified rather than filled in from assumption.
The legal ceiling is identical whoever the owner is. Nothing in this section changes the 1.6% / banked analysis on the Calculations page.

California's statewide Tenant Protection Act covers many corporate owners, but in San Francisco the local 1.6% is stricter, so the local rule controls (S25, Sec. 1947.12(d)(3)). A common misconception is that a larger owner may use the state cap instead. It may not, in this city.

rows.large_owner: 1.6% of base rent for 3/1/26-2/28/27, plus properly banked amounts.
rows.individual_owner: Identical. No institutional exemption or alternative cap exists.

rows.large_owner: Only by Rent Board petition: capital improvement, O&M (up to 7%), utility passthrough, special circumstances/comparable rents.
rows.individual_owner: Identical petition routes. Filing a petition is free for either owner.

rows.large_owner: Once every 12 months; 30 days' notice, or 90 days if the increase exceeds 10%.

Revenue-management / algorithmic pricing tools that use non-public competitor data are banned in San Francisco. Owners using such tools had to change practice when Sec. 37.10C took effect on October 14, 2024. Penalty: up to $1,000 per violation, per unit, per month.

rows.topic: A practice that is banned but was historically common among large owners
rows.large_owner: Rent-setting software marketed on peer-landlord data. Now unlawful in San Francisco. This is the only documented, sourced statement this site can make about large-owner conduct.
rows.individual_owner: Not documented in any source located.

rows.topic: How large owners otherwise set the amount
rows.note: No official source describes this. Nothing is filled in.

rows.topic: How individual owners otherwise set the amount
rows.note: No official source describes this. Nothing is filled in.

rows.large_owner: The rent increase licence: reporting into the Housing Inventory annually by March 1. A notice is unenforceable without a licence in effect on the effective date.
rows.individual_owner: The same licence requirement, plus the 90-day notice rule when a banked increase pushes the total above 10%.
rows.note: This row identifies the two rules easiest to breach in these particular facts. It is not a statistic and no rate of non-compliance is claimed.

rows.topic: Dispute route available to the tenant
rows.large_owner: Free Rent Board petition (no time limit); free Rent Board ADR; City-listed free tenant counsellors; free legal representation through the Tenant Right to Counsel program at the eviction stage.
rows.individual_owner: Identical. The same free resources apply regardless of the owner's size.

rows.note: No defensible ZIP-level market rent was obtained. HUD's interactive FMR lookup returned an empty result in this session and the Census API required a key. No market figure is used anywhere on this site, and none is needed: the lawful cap does not depend on market rent.

secondary_sources.title: San Francisco Rent Increase 2026: What the 1.6% Allowable Increase Means for Landlords and Tenants
secondary_sources.note: Commercial source, fetched 2026-11-06. It agrees with the Rent Board on 1.6% and on the missing October 2025 CPI as the reason for the estimated figure, and explains the geometric-mean method. It does NOT describe how owners set rents, so it is not cited for that. Retained here only as corroboration of the 1.6% figure.
